lessons.title: Cybersecurity foundations and the CIA triad
lessons.subtitle: Understand confidentiality, integrity, availability, assets, threats, weaknesses, impact and layered controls.
lessons.description: Understand confidentiality, integrity, availability, assets, threats, weaknesses, impact and layered controls. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 1 — Cybersecurity foundations and the CIA triad

LEARNING OUTCOME
Understand confidentiality, integrity, availability, assets, threats, weaknesses, impact and layered controls.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. The security goal

Cybersecurity keeps information and systems trustworthy while allowing the right people to use them. Confidentiality limits disclosure; integrity protects correctness; availability keeps required services usable. These aims can conflict: a strict access rule may protect confidentiality while accidentally blocking legitimate work. Begin with the business purpose, the asset, and the acceptable risk rather than buying tools first.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — CIA triad. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Asset inventory. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Threat, weakness, impact and control

A threat is a possible cause of harm; a vulnerability is a weakness that could be used or triggered; impact is the consequence; a control reduces likelihood or impact. A bug or alert is not proof that a breach occurred, and an alert is not proof a particular person is responsible. Separate verified facts, hypotheses and conclusions.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Threat path. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Layered controls. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Layered defensive practice

Start with an inventory, unique accounts, MFA, timely updates, protected and tested backups, secure configuration, monitoring and a response plan. Assign an owner to each control and test whether it works. Security maturity is built by making fundamental safeguards repeatable and reviewing them, not by assuming one product stops every threat.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Risk equation. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Recovery cycle. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Guided practice — learn by doing

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.output: A fictional asset record helps focus the security plan.

lessons.title: Asset inventory, threat modeling and risk
lessons.subtitle: Identify important assets, model plausible failure paths, estimate likelihood and impact, and assign risk treatments.
lessons.description: Identify important assets, model plausible failure paths, estimate likelihood and impact, and assign risk treatments. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 2 — Asset inventory, threat modeling and risk

LEARNING OUTCOME
Identify important assets, model plausible failure paths, estimate likelihood and impact, and assign risk treatments.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Inventory before scoring

Record each service, data handled, business purpose, owner, exposure, dependencies and recovery needs. Classify data by sensitivity, not curiosity. Keep inventories in approved workspaces and remove unneeded copies. Unknown or ownerless assets are hard to protect because nobody can make a decision about them.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Asset map. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Threat source. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Model plausible events

Ask what could go wrong, what assumptions must be true, what weak points exist, and what could prevent or detect the event. Structured models such as STRIDE can help brainstorm, but they do not prove a threat will occur. Include outages, misconfiguration, accidental deletion, supplier failures and mistakes as well as malicious events.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Weakness path. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Likelihood × impact. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Treat risk with ownership

Estimate likelihood and impact using the organization’s agreed scale and document uncertainty. Risk can be mitigated, avoided, transferred in part, or consciously accepted by an accountable owner with a review date. A numeric score supports judgement; it does not replace judgement.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Risk register. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Treatment options. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

lessons.title: Identity, authentication, MFA and least privilege
lessons.subtitle: Design safer access, strong authentication, account recovery and regular privilege review.
lessons.description: Design safer access, strong authentication, account recovery and regular privilege review. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 3 — Identity, authentication, MFA and least privilege

LEARNING OUTCOME
Design safer access, strong authentication, account recovery and regular privilege review.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Authentication and authorization differ

Authentication answers “who is this identity?” Authorization answers “what may it do?” A successful sign-in must not automatically grant access to every record. Enforce authorization on the server for each protected action, even if a user modifies a URL or submits an API request directly.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Identity flow. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — MFA layers. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Build resilient sign-in

Use unique accounts, MFA or passkeys where supported, secure recovery, appropriate session expiry and alerts for risky changes. Store passwords with a vetted password-specific hashing scheme and unique salts; never save raw passwords or log secrets. Unexpected MFA prompts should be denied and reported.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Least privilege. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Role mapping. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Review access as a lifecycle

Joiner-mover-leaver processes create, change, review and remove access. Service identities need owners and narrow permissions; rotate or revoke exposed credentials. Periodic access reviews should be evidence-based and record who approved exceptions.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Account lifecycle. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Access review. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

lessons.subtitle: Understand ports, protocols, trust zones and how to apply safe, staged firewall rules.
lessons.description: Understand ports, protocols, trust zones and how to apply safe, staged firewall rules. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 4 — Network fundamentals, segmentation and firewalls

LEARNING OUTCOME
Understand ports, protocols, trust zones and how to apply safe, staged firewall rules.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Read a network clearly

An IP address identifies a network interface in context; a port identifies an application endpoint; a protocol defines communication behavior. An open port is not automatically a vulnerability. Determine whether the service is expected, patched, authenticated, monitored and reachable only by the intended clients.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Traffic path. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Network zones. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Make firewall policy explicit

A firewall evaluates traffic attributes such as direction, source, destination, protocol and port. Start from the service inventory, deny by default, and allow only required flows. Keep public web services separate from internal databases, administration paths and backups.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Firewall rule. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Allow-list. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Change safely

Before changing a remote firewall, verify recovery access, document dependencies, test in a lab and prepare a rollback. Check both IPv4 and IPv6 policy, inspect logs, and record exceptions with owners and expiry dates. An overly broad rule can cause outages even when it is not directly exploitable.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Stateful inspection. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Rule review. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Guided practice — learn by doing

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

approved_flows = [("internet", "web-gateway", 443), ("web-gateway", "app", 8443)]

lessons.title: Endpoint hardening, patching and backups
lessons.subtitle: Reduce attack surface and prove that backups can restore important services.
lessons.description: Reduce attack surface and prove that backups can restore important services. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 5 — Endpoint hardening, patching and backups

LEARNING OUTCOME
Reduce attack surface and prove that backups can restore important services.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Shrink the attack surface

Endpoints include laptops, phones, workstations and servers. Remove unnecessary software and services, standardize secure configurations, remove defaults, restrict local administrator rights and enable appropriate protection. A baseline provides a repeatable state to compare against.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Endpoint baseline. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Patch cycle. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Patch through a lifecycle

Inventory systems, evaluate vendor guidance and exploitation evidence, prioritize exposure, test updates, deploy in waves and verify success. Track unsupported platforms as a risk needing migration, isolation or a documented plan. A deadline is meaningless if nobody measures whether updates installed.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Attack surface. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Backup tiers. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Backups must be restorable

Keep separate protected copies and restrict who can modify or delete them. Test restores, record recovery time and recovery point objectives, and ensure backup credentials are not casually reachable from normal sessions. Recovery exercises include people and dependencies, not just files.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Restore test. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Hardening review. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

lessons.subtitle: Protect information in transit and at rest, manage keys responsibly, and prevent secret leakage.
lessons.description: Protect information in transit and at rest, manage keys responsibly, and prevent secret leakage. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 6 — Encryption, TLS, data classification and secrets

LEARNING OUTCOME
Protect information in transit and at rest, manage keys responsibly, and prevent secret leakage.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Classify data first

Identify public, internal, confidential and highly restricted data. Collect only what is needed and limit retention and access. Encryption at rest can help protect a lost disk; TLS protects data in transit. Neither replaces correct authorization or makes a compromised application safe.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Data lifecycle. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — TLS in transit. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Understand TLS

HTTPS uses TLS to provide confidentiality, integrity and authentication for a network connection. Browsers validate certificate chains and hostnames. Investigate expired, mismatched or untrusted certificates instead of teaching users to click through warnings. Monitor renewals and use current server guidance.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Encryption at rest. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Key lifecycle. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Manage secrets as secrets

API tokens, keys, database passwords and recovery codes must stay out of source control, screenshots, client-side code and logs. Use an approved secret store, restrict scope, name an owner, rotate when exposed and revoke unused credentials. If a key leaks, rotate it; deleting a line is not enough.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Secret storage. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Rotation schedule. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Guided practice — learn by doing

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

print(record, classification)

lessons.title: Logging, monitoring, detection and incident response
lessons.subtitle: Make useful records, validate alerts, preserve evidence and coordinate recovery.
lessons.description: Make useful records, validate alerts, preserve evidence and coordinate recovery. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 7 — Logging, monitoring, detection and incident response

LEARNING OUTCOME
Make useful records, validate alerts, preserve evidence and coordinate recovery.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Logs should answer questions

Useful logs help show what happened, when, to which asset and through which identity. Collect sign-in events, permission changes, administrative actions, security alerts and key application errors. Use consistent timestamps and protect logs from tampering. Avoid logging raw passwords, tokens, sensitive request bodies or unnecessary personal data.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Log pipeline. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Detection rule. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Triage using evidence

An alert is a signal to investigate. Validate data sources, asset identity, time window and business context; correlate sources before making a conclusion. Rate urgency based on impact, scope, active exposure and confidence, and document the reasoning for the next analyst.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Alert triage. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Incident phases. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Respond with roles

Define who can declare an incident, isolate a system, preserve evidence, contact leadership and approve recovery. Containment should be coordinated; hasty deletion can destroy evidence or interrupt services. After recovery, find the root cause, close weaknesses, and update controls and playbooks.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Evidence custody. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Lessons learned. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Lesson 8 — Secure web applications and OWASP risks

LEARNING OUTCOME
Protect web requests, authorization, sessions, data queries, output and dependencies.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Follow the request lifecycle

A web app receives input, authenticates the caller, authorizes the action, applies business rules, accesses data and returns a response. Security belongs at every stage. Client-side checks improve experience but can be bypassed, so validate on the server with expected formats and limits.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Request flow. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Validate input. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Enforce access per action

Check permissions on every sensitive request and scope each data query to the signed-in identity or approved role. Use secure session settings, rotate session IDs after sign-in, set appropriate Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite cookie attributes, and avoid exposing tokens in URLs.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Authorize action. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Secure session. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Use secure implementation patterns

Encode untrusted output for its context, use parameterized database queries, apply CSRF protection where relevant, keep dependencies updated and avoid verbose production errors. Use code review, threat modeling and testing before launch; use monitoring after deployment.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Encode output. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Test and fix. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Guided practice — learn by doing

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.output: Toy validation only; never use a client-side check as the only authorization.

blocks.text: Lesson 9 — Cloud security, IAM and configuration hygiene

LEARNING OUTCOME
Secure cloud identities, network boundaries, storage policies, audit trails and configuration changes.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Understand shared responsibility

Cloud providers secure parts of the underlying platform, while customers retain responsibilities for identities, data, configuration, workloads and applications. Exact responsibilities depend on the service model. Write down each control owner and alert recipient.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Shared responsibility. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Cloud identity. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Identity and boundaries first

Use MFA, role-based access, short-lived credentials, scoped service identities and separation of development and production. Review public exposure, inbound rules, storage access, encryption settings and backups. Prefer reviewed infrastructure-as-code and automated policy checks over undocumented console changes.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Network boundary. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Storage policy. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Detect configuration drift

Small changes can expose storage or grant excessive privileges. Log administrative changes, alert on high-impact drift, use approved templates and test incident and restore procedures. Use fabricated secrets and data in lessons; never paste real production keys into tutorial code.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Audit trail. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Config review. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Guided practice — learn by doing

Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

print([k for k,v in policy.items() if not v])

blocks.text: Lesson 10 — Cybersecurity capstone: design a safer organization

LEARNING OUTCOME
Create a measured plan combining risk, controls, owners, response exercises and review.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Plan outcomes, not purchases

Use a fictional organization. Identify its important data and services, list risks, select a few controls, assign owners and define how success will be measured. Use NIST CSF to organize outcomes rather than treating a framework as a list of products.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Governance. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Protect controls. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Measure safeguards

Examples include account MFA coverage, critical patch compliance, restore-test success, alert acknowledgement time, and closure rate for validated findings. State a baseline, target, data source, owner and review cadence. Metrics should support decisions, not reward misleading numbers.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Detect signals. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Response plan. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Exercise and improve

Run a tabletop for a lost device, compromised administrator session or service outage. Keep it simulated, notify participants and avoid real customer data. Record decisions, identify missing contacts, update the response plan and schedule a follow-up review.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Recovery target. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Measure progress. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.
